en: *Pratimālakṣaṇavivaraṇam*:
Oṃ... Whatever fruit was spoken of by the Blessed One regarding the form of the Buddha, that very characteristic of the Buddha-images is here likewise set down.
An image complete with all the auspicious marks bestows happiness;
whereas one devoid of them, because of that deficiency, will at the end bring about suffering.
What is that happiness?

He says: however many atoms there are in the stūpas or images of the Blessed One, for that much time the maker [of the image] will certainly enjoy sovereignty on earth and in heaven; and having experienced all this—even without the perfection of a throne of form—he attains the state of a Buddha, which is free from birth, old age, and misfortune.

Therefore, he states the characteristics of the form body (*rūpakāya*): therein, for the Perfectly Awakened Ones (*samyaksambuddhas*) and the Great Vajra-holders (*mahāvajradharas*), what is the measure of the body’s length, including the span of the two arms extended at the sides?
It is twelve and a half finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) per *tāla*; thus, it is one hundred and twenty-five finger-breadths.

For the goddesses such as Locanā and the others, it is twelve finger-breadths per *tāla*; thus, with nine *tālas*, their height and the span of their arms (*vyāma*) is one hundred and eight finger-breadths.
For Bodhisattvas, it is exactly ten *tālas* of twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*) each.
For the dwarfish, pot-bellied, and wrathful deities, it is ninety-six finger-breadths, or eight *tālas*.
For the playfully wrathful deities, however, it is ten *tālas*, and their height and span should be known as one hundred and twenty finger-breadths, with all major and minor limbs fully developed.

At the time of the Teacher’s departure for the teaching of the Dharma, Śāriputra said this to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, in the absence of the Blessed One, how should faithful sons of good family and daughters of good family practice?

The Blessed One said: “Śāriputra! When I have departed or entered parinirvāṇa, images should be made for the sake of worship and honor, with a body as wide as a *vyāma* and as high as a *vyāma*, just like the circumference of a *nyagrodha* tree; and as long as the body is, so long shall the *vyāma* be.”

The excellent proportions consist of the fullness, beauty, grace, and elegance of all the primary limbs (*aṅga*), secondary limbs (*upāṅga*), and parts (*avayava*); the seven protuberances; the large jaw; and the well-situated uṣṇīṣa on the head and shoulders, which are shaped like a parasol.

Regarding this, it is said: "In that regard, the measurement of the forms of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas is determined by their length, width, height, the articulation of the joints, and the projections."
In this context, *lāvaṇya* is the quality of being smooth;
*lālitya* is charm;
and *salīlatva* is due to qualities such as the three-fold bend (*tribhaṅga*).
"Seven protuberances" refers to seven parts.
"Protuberances," "elevations," and "prominences" are synonyms.
Which are they? They are the two feet, the two hands, the two shoulders, and the neck.
Furthermore, it is well known that some degree of height (*ucchraya*) is required.

Therein, the *uṣṇīṣa* and the location of the hair are four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*). Likewise, from the forehead and nose down to the chin, it is four finger-breadths plus a quarter. By this, the portion of the face measures twelve and a half units (*mātrā*).
The chin should be two finger-breadths [in thickness];
it is desired to be four finger-breadths in both length and projection.
The two cheeks should be four finger-breadths wide, extending out from the root of the ear.
The jaw should be below the lower part of the skin covering the eyes; it should be two finger-breadths in height and two finger-breadths in width. This measurement is with respect to a Bodhisattva.
The jaw should be full like that of a great lion;
this means it is slightly elevated in the case of the Perfectly Awakened Ones and the Great Vajra-holders,
whereas for the wrathful deities (*krodha*), it is flat and wider than it is high.
The lower lip is two finger-breadths in length, with its projection and thickness being one *mātrikā*.
One *mātrikā* is defined as one-third of a finger-breadth.
The middle of the lower lip should be like the fruit of the *bimba* tree.
The corners of the mouth are one finger-breadth [in width].
The face is four finger-breadths in length, with its features arranged as they naturally occur, and it possesses forty teeth in the sequence beginning with the central upper incisors.
The upper lip—
The protrusion and height [of the nose] are each four barley-corns (yava) and half a finger-breadth (aṅgula).
From the tip of the nose to the lower lip is eight fingers; the line for the mustache is one-third of that, shaped like a *praṇīla*.
The *godhi* (the area between the nostrils) has a width of two fingers and a height of two and a half fingers.
In the Buddhas, it is slightly larger;
in those who are excessively wrathful, it is somewhat flattened and protrudes from the side;
and in others, the two channels are circular and equal to half a finger-breadth.
The bridge of her nose is straight, and its tip is half an aṅgula in width;
the socket of the eye is four aṅgulas.
In the middle of that, it is one *aṅgula* in width; in the center, it is two *aṅgulas*.
Starting from below the eyebrows down to the lower limit, it is three *aṅgulis*.
Between the eyes, the root of the nose is one *aṅgula*; the eyebrows are four *aṅgulas* long and shaped like a bow.
The [line] of Vajradhara is half a finger-breadth in width at the center; that of the wrathful deities is curved;

that of the Buddhas, whose gaze is in meditative absorption, is bow-shaped with a width of two barley-corns and a length of two fingers plus six barley-corns; while that of the Bodhisattvas is shaped like an utpala flower, with a width of four barley-corns and a length of twenty barley-corns.
For all women of the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic) type, [the nose] is eighteen *yava*s in length and six *yava*s in width, having the shape of a fish's belly (*matsyodara*).
The space near the nostrils is four *yava*s; this is the end of one eye, and the other end of the eye is likewise.
The *pāṅga* consists of four barley grains;
the *cakṣurmaṇi* is three finger-breadths wide and raised by two barley grains due to its protuberance.
The *kālikā* measures slightly more than five barleycorns; the line from the corner of the mouth (*sṛkkaṇī*) to the eye is the same length, with a small doll-like mark (*puttalikā*) in the middle.
Its width is one-fifth of a half-finger, and the pupil (*tārā*) is one-third of that.
The white circle of the eye (*akṣiputraka*) is revealed to be a fourth part of a finger-breadth.
The eye-socket should be shaped like a lotus petal and measure three finger-breadths;
the suture of the nostril should be equal to that of the *karavīra* flower.
The chin and the corners of the mouth are equal to a tāla; the space between the eyebrows is one and a half finger-breadths (aṅgulas);
and right there, the ūrṇā-hair is one finger-breadth, resembling the full moon.
The nose, the ūrṇā, and the uṣṇīṣa are equal in measurement. The two ears are like the line of the eyebrows;
they are four finger-breadths in length and two finger-breadths in width, and their lobe is one barley-corn in thickness.
The upper leaf of those two is four barley-corns wide and bent upwards one finger-breadth;
the cavity is four barley-corns wide.
Between the cheek and the ear-opening, the ear-whorl is shaped like a *phalika* fruit and measures two barley-corns.
The ear-leaf (*karṇalatā*) is four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length; it is thick and beautiful as is fitting.

Having previously described the measurement from the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*) down to the neck as twenty-four finger-breadths plus four barley-corns (*yava*), the division now proceeds from the neck down to below the ankle.
The neck (*grīvā*) is four finger-breadths.
From the neck to the heart is twelve and a half finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
From the heart to the end of the navel, and likewise from the navel to the private parts, is twelve and a half finger-breadths.
The thigh is twenty-five finger-breadths.
The shank is likewise;
the knee is six finger-breadths [in length];
the ankle is two finger-breadths.

The measurement of ten *tālas* for the Fully Enlightened Buddhas, Vajradharas, Bodhisattvas, and others, is explained as extending four finger-breadths below the ankles. For others, however, it should be inferred according to what is appropriate.
The crown jewel should be made spotless and as beautiful as possible.
Taking the *uṣṇīṣa* as the central point, the crown of matted hair (*jaṭāmakuṭa*) of Vajradhara is twelve finger-widths (*aṅgula*) long.
For the heroic Bodhisattvas, the matted hair-bun (*jaṭājūṭa*) and crown are eight finger-widths long; this is the distinction.
Some say it is ten finger-widths.
Twelve finger-breadths below the uṣṇīṣa, it is encircled;
above the forehead, it has the shape of a parasol;
its upward-pointing tuft is blue and curls to the right.
With the head elevated by encircling it from behind up to the ears, the head measures thirty-two finger-breadths;
the neck is eight finger-breadths in width.
Its circumference is twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).

Leaving eight finger-breadths from the neck, the circle of the shoulder near the ear is twelve finger-breadths, including four finger-breadths [from the neck], and it is provided with a pillar-base (*sthāṇukṣoṇī*).
From the shoulder, which is free from thinness, the upper arm (*bāhu*) above the elbow (*kaphoṇi*) is twenty finger-breadths, and the elbow is one finger-breadth.
The forearm (prabāhu), from below the elbow to above the wrist, is sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgulas) long.
The wrist (maṇibandha) is one finger-breadth.
The hand (hasta), from below the wrist to the tip of the middle finger, is twelve finger-breadths long.
Thus, [the circumference] at the fifty-finger-width [point] is twenty finger-widths for the encirclement at the middle of the upper arm,
and sixteen finger-widths for the encirclement at the middle of the forearm.
The wrist-wrap is twelve finger-breadths [in length].
The palm is seven finger-breadths from the wrist.
The middle finger is five mātrās [in length].
Its index finger is shorter by one joint;
the ring finger is equal to that;
the little finger is shorter by one joint.
All the fingers have three joints;
their nails are half the length of a joint.
Leaving four finger-breadths from the wrist, the thumb is four finger-breadths long, ending at the tip of its nail.
The nail consists of two joints, or half a joint;
the thumb is four finger-breadths in circumference;
and the distance between the thumb and the forefinger is three finger-breadths.
From the wrist to the base of the little finger is five finger-breadths (pañcāṅgula).
From the shoulder to the armpit is nine finger-breadths.
From the armpit to the breast is six finger-breadths.
The circumference of the chest and back is fifty-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas).
The distance between the two breasts is twelve and a half finger-breadths.
The distance between the breasts and the navel is sixteen finger-breadths.

Starting from the navel, extending backward along with the spine as far as the navel, it measures forty-six finger-breadths; the depressions at the navel are one finger-breadth deep and one finger-breadth in circumference.
Likewise, the waist is eighteen finger-breadths in width, and the two buttocks are four finger-breadths each in width and length.
The space between the two testicles is twelve finger-breadths;
when measured by its circumference, it is three times that.
In the middle of those two, the scrotal sacs are five finger-breadths in length and four finger-breadths in width.
Above that, the secret organ is two finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in width; in length, it is six finger-breadths plus two barley-corns (yavas).
The middle of the thighs is thirty-two finger-breadths in circumference, and the circumference of the knees is twenty-eight finger-breadths.
The circumference at the middle of the shank is twenty-four finger-breadths;
the circumference below the shank is twenty-one finger-breadths;
and the heel below the ankle joint is four finger-breadths.
Below and above, it measures six finger-breadths;
in lateral width and circumference, it is eighteen finger-breadths; from below the ankle...
From the tips of the big toe nails down to the feet, they are twelve finger-breadths in width and six finger-breadths in height;
the heels of the feet are two finger-breadths in width from bottom to top;
and the five toes have two joints each.
The nails are half the length of their middle joints.
The big toe is five *aṅgulas* in circumference and three *aṅgulas* in length; the second toe is equal to that.
The middle finger is one and a half joints shorter than that;
the ring finger is one-eighth part shorter than that;
and the little finger is also one-eighth part shorter than that.
The fingers are raised by one finger-breadth;
the tips of the two thumbs are raised by one and a half finger-breadths;
the feet are turned upward on the outside and are level with the back of a tortoise.
Adorned at the bottom with wheels and other symbols,
the mandala is square, shaped like a hen’s egg or a sesame seed;
the facial forms of all common lingas are of four types.
The faces of the perfectly awakened ones and the Great Vajradharas are shaped like the eggs of a hen;
those of the divine maidens such as Locanā and others are shaped like sesame seeds;
and the faces of the great bodhisattvas such as Maitreya and others are like those of the Great Vajradharas.
For those who are short, pot-bellied, and wrathful, the face is circular in shape;
for those with graceful wrath, however, it is like that of a Bodhisattva;
while for pretas and the like, the face is square.
The two faces have a beautiful appearance;
the two faces are square-shaped and deformed in aspect. The gaze is even.
"With faces serene, with gentle and affectionate gazes,
and half-bowed with humility,
one should stand below the All-Seeing Ones. Thus it is said.

By wrapping [the cloth] around the crown, the secret place, the thighs, and the back of the Yoginīs such as Locanā and the others, their full and firm breasts are formed together with ten finger-breadths. By wrapping it around the navel and excluding one-tenth part, the hip region should be made full. According to the measurement of a Bodhisattva, the chest of the Vīriṇīs is [formed] by one-tenth part from the breast and one part from the secret place.
The pair of breasts and the region of the waist are as before;
for the crow-faced goddesses and others, there is fullness at the breasts and other parts by means of two tālas each.

In the previously described characteristics of the Blessed One Śrī Saṃvara, having set aside four *yavas* from the field of the face, and within a width consisting of twelve parts, the faces of the Blessed One—the root, left, right, and western—are formed by drawing [the lines] after removing one and a half, two and a half, and two parts respectively at the lower corners. The faces of Vajravārāhī, Khaṇḍarohā, Rūpiṇī, and the Devakanyās are like the seed-syllable *tila* in shape, resembling the western face of the Blessed One; the face of Ḍākinī is like the eastern face [of the Blessed One]; that of Lāmā is like the left face; and [that of Khandarohā is like the right face].

The [deities] beginning with Kākāsyā have faces like crows and so forth; the specific distinction is that they make the left and right faces of the Bhagavat appear as if laughing, terrified, or hungry, resembling the luster of a mango. Indra, Īśāna, Vāyu, Varuṇa, Upendra, and Pitāmaha are nine tālas in height and have faces like bird-eggs.
Vemacitrin and Nairṛti are six tālas in height and possess a wrathful nature;
Kubera and Anala are eight tālas tall, being graceful and short respectively, with bird-like and egg-shaped faces.
The gentle planets and the Sun are honored with the same proportions as Śakra.
The cruel ones are those whose nature is anger.
Rāhu has half a body;
Ketu has the form of a nāga in its lower body.
All nāgas are nine *tālas* with faces like the eggs of birds.
A student (*baṭu*), a dwarf (*vāmana*), and Heramba are to be made five *tālas*.
In that system, the face is one *tāla*; from the neck to the genitals is two *tālas*; and from the genitals to the soles of the feet is two *tālas*—thus it is five *tālas*.
In that regard, the Perfect Buddhas are endowed with the peaceful rasa of compassion, while their entire body has the face of Vajradhara and is permeated by the nine rasas;
however, the Bodhisattvas and others are characterized primarily by the erotic rasa—thus is the arrangement described.
Thus ends the Exposition on the Characteristics of Images, spoken by the Perfectly Awakened One.
These are their intrinsic natures: Rāhu has the form of half a body;
Ketu has the form of a nāga in its lower body.
All the *nāgas* are nine *tālas* with beaks like those of birds.
A student (*baṭu*), a dwarf (*vāmana*), and Heramba should be made five *tālas*.
In that system, the face is one *tāla*; from the neck to the genitals is two *tālas*; and from the genitals to the soles of the feet is two *tālas*—thus it is five *tālas*.
Therein, the perfectly enlightened ones, endowed with the essence of compassion and the flavor of peace, have their entire body as the face of Vajradhara.
